paper.title: The Myth of Nordic Mobility: Social Mobility Rates in Modern Denmark and Sweden
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project number is given. …

registers.role: sample frame, vertical and horizontal kinship linkage, and the years-of-education (and income) measures for Denmark

registers.name_in_paper: Swedish Population Register (via Collado et al. 2023, Table 3)
registers.role: source of the Swedish observed kin correlations in years of education used in Table 1

registers.name_in_paper: OECD PISA 2018 Results (Volume I), tables 1.B1.1-6, pp. 216-21
registers.role: country-level standard deviations of Mathematics, Reading and Science scores, the y-variable of Figure 2

registers.name_in_paper: Gini coefficient for disposable income, averaged 2012-2022 (source not named)

linkages: Administrative records covering both vertical and horizontal family linkages, used to compute correlations across kinship relations such as uncle to niece, father to son-in-law and brother to sister-in-law
Kinship defined on biological links: a man and a woman are considered spouses if they have a child together
Spouses in Table 1 are defined as individuals who are parents of a given child, with no implication that either played a role in raising the child
Siblings are full siblings only - children who shared a father and mother
Inclusion in the Danish sample required that both parents have an ID in the register

sample.universe: Denmark: the full population in the Danish Population Register born before 1985. Sweden: a 35 percent random sample of individuals born between 1932 and 1967 from the Swedish Population Register, taken from Collado et al. (2023, Table 3).
sample.unit_of_observation: pair of relatives (kinship pair); one correlation is computed per relationship type, pooling pairs irrespective of gender
selection_rules: Denmark: born prior to 1985, so that education would overwhelmingly be complete

Denmark: both parents must have an ID in the register (the register was introduced in 1968, so only Danish residents still living in 1968 are guaranteed to be included), which leaves the younger part of the population with an average birth year of 1967
Denmark: at maximum 2.3 million individuals are included
Sweden: 35 percent random sample of individuals born between 1932 and 1967 (as drawn by Collado et al. 2023)
sample.n_observations: Table 1 pair counts, Denmark: 650,723 (cousins) to 4,241,096 (parent-child); Sweden: 413,062 (spouses) to 2,427,198 (siblings-in-law)

construction_notes: Years of education has been standardized to the same mean and standard deviation by birth cohort and by gender
The reported correlation in Table 1 is the average correlation within each relationship-type, irrespective of gender
Standard errors of the Table 1 correlations are computed as SE = sqrt((1 - rho^2)/(N - 1))
Standard errors in Table 2 are computed using the Delta method; for a ratio X/Y, SE_{X/Y} = (1/mu_Y) * sqrt(sigma_X^2 + (mu_X^2/mu_Y^2) sigma_Y^2) (Appendix 2)
Table 2 reports the ratios of the Table 1 correlations that identify b, r and s, plus an unweighted average across kinship types

Appendix 1 simulations use 1 million random draws of underlying status for parent, child and marital partner, with a parent-child and marital correlation in underlying status of 0.8 and normally distributed underlying status; measured status is then transformed into classical-error, rank (0-100), five-class, top-50% indicator, top-5% indicator and lognormal forms
Income was also used as the outcome; because of clear gender differences in income correlations across relatives, the income estimation uses male relatives only

claims.statement: In the Danish register data the observed correlation in standardized completed years of education between an individual and the individual's spouse (the other parent of their child) is 0.443; under the paper's measurement-error model this observed correlation equals θr.

treatment.label: Standardized completed years of education of the individual's spouse (the other parent of their child)

register_source.value: Danish Population Register (no DST register code or variable name given in the paper)

definition.value: Completed years of education of the relative, standardized to the same mean and standard deviation by birth cohort and by gender. Kinship is defined on biological links; spouses are two people who have a child together and siblings are full siblings only.

timing.value: Measured once education is complete; the Danish sample is restricted to people born before 1985 for that reason.

outcome.label: Standardized completed years of education of the focal individual

register_source.value: Danish Population Register (no DST register code or variable name given in the paper)

definition.value: Completed years of education of the focal individual, standardized to the same mean and standard deviation by birth cohort and by gender. The reported figure is the average correlation within the relationship type, irrespective of gender.

timing.value: Measured once education is complete; sample restricted to births before 1985.

units.value: Pearson correlation coefficient in standardized completed years of education (unit-free)

estimand.target_population: Pairs of relatives of this type in the Danish population born before 1985 with both parents identified in the register (average birth year 1967)

population.description: Danish Population Register, full population born before 1985, both parents having a register ID; 1,869,156 pairs of this relationship type
population.selection: Both parents must have an ID in the population register (introduced 1968), which leaves the younger part of the Danish population, with an average birth year of 1967

identification.source_of_variation: None: this is the observed (measurement-error attenuated) correlation between relatives in the register, the input from which the underlying correlations are later identified by ratios.

key_assumptions.assumption: Spousal choice (marital assortment) is made independently of the status of the parents or siblings, i.e. matching is on the characteristics of the marital partners alone, so that the parent to child-in-law correlation equals θbr
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as 'entirely plausible' for modern Nordic countries (p. 4); no empirical test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Kinship is defined on biological links: a man and a woman are counted as spouses if they have a child together, and siblings are full siblings only
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the definition used, following Collado et al. (2023); the paper notes there is no implication that either parent raised the child.

threats_discussed: Years of education is a loose indicator of underlying educational ability, so observed kin correlations are attenuated by measurement error

The degree to which years of education signals underlying ability varies across societies (e.g. an 81% Danish tertiary completion rate against 56% in the USA), so raw cross-country comparisons of mobility are not comparable
Measurement errors may be non-classical and non-normal; years of education and income show marked clumping on particular values, and category measures of status are worse
Attenuation may differ across male-male, male-female and female-female pairs
The Danish sample is selected on both parents having a register ID, leaving the younger part of the population
robustness_checks: Re-estimation using male-only kinship types (p. 7): b 0.70, s 0.70, r 0.78 against 0.68, 0.67, 0.79 with all gender pairings

Multiple independent kinship ratios for the same parameter (child-in-law, aunt/uncle, sibling-in-law, cousin, sibling of sibling-in-law, spouse of sibling-in-law, parent-parent-in-law, aunt/uncle-in-law)
Simulations with non-normal / non-classical measurement error (Appendix 1, Table 4)
Income used as an alternative status measure (p. 8)
Comparison with the 20-parameter latent-status model of Collado et al. (2023) fitted to 105 Swedish correlations

estimator.value: Pearson correlation between relatives within the relationship type, pooled irrespective of gender; standard error computed as SE = sqrt((1 - rho^2)/(N - 1))

estimation.specification: Correlation of standardized completed years of education between the two members of each spouse pair; no controls, no fixed effects

source_table.value: Table 1, Denmark columns, row 'Spouse'

heterogeneity.finding: The reported correlation is the average within the relationship type irrespective of gender; the paper reports separately that restricting to male-only kinship ties yields nearly identical implied parameters.

ambiguities: Table 1 prints no significance stars or p-values; statistically_significant is recorded as true on the basis of the printed correlation and its standard error (the ratio exceeds 100 for every Danish row).
The paper names no DST register code or variable name; 'Danish Population Register' is mapped to BEF at the data level only.
theory_referenced: Latent underlying social status with classical measurement error (y = x + u), status being indexed only imperfectly by years of education, income, wealth or occupational status
Multiplicative kin-correlation structure of status transmission with assortative mating (as in Collado et al. 2023)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text and in Fig. 1: because the attenuation enters each observed kin correlation once, it appears identically in the numerator and denominator of every ratio. No separate test.

population.description: Danish Population Register, full population born before 1985, both parents having a register ID; at maximum 2.3 million individuals
subgroups_defined: male-only kinship ties (reported in the text, p. 7)
population.selection: Both parents must have an ID in the population register (introduced 1968), which leaves the younger part of the Danish population, with an average birth year of 1967

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation: the underlying correlation is identified by dividing the observed correlation between relatives at one place in the family tree by that between relatives at another, so that the common measurement-error attenuation θ cancels. Here unweighted average of the kinship-ratio estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The measurement-error attenuation factor θ is the same for every partial indicator of social status and for every kinship pair, whether the pair is a single link (siblings) or a chain of links (brother to sister-in-law), so that θ cancels when one kin correlation is divided by another
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text and in Fig. 1: because the attenuation enters each observed kin correlation once, it appears identically in the numerator and denominator of every ratio. No separate test.

key_assumptions.assumption: Classical measurement error: measured status is y = x + u, the error u being independent of underlying status x
key_assumptions.supported_by: Simulations in Appendix 1 / Table 4 show the ratio method still recovers the underlying correlations for rank, five-class, dichotomous and lognormal status measures.

key_assumptions.assumption: The attenuation factor θ is the same across the gender combinations of the relative pair; and even if male-male, male-female and female-female attenuations differ, the average attenuation θ = (1/4)(φ + ω + 2τ) enters numerator and denominator of each ratio in the same way
key_assumptions.supported_by: Male-only kinship estimates reported in the text (p. 7) give nearly identical values (b 0.70, s 0.70, r 0.78 against 0.68, 0.67, 0.79 with all gender pairings).

key_assumptions.assumption: Underlying social status and the measurement errors are normally distributed
key_assumptions.supported_by: Simulations in Appendix 1 / Table 4 with rank, social-class, dichotomous and lognormal status measures.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: inclusion in the Danish data requires that both parents have an ID in the population register (introduced 1968) and that the person was born before 1985, which selects the younger part of the Danish population (average birth year 1967)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the text; the paper reports the resulting average birth year (1967) and maximum sample size (2.3 million) but offers no test of selectivity.

key_assumptions.assumption: People born before 1985 have overwhelmingly completed their education, so completed years of education is observed for them
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the reason for the 1985 birth cut-off; no completion check reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Kinship is defined on biological links: a man and a woman are counted as spouses if they have a child together, and siblings are full siblings only
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the definition used, following Collado et al. (2023); the paper notes there is no implication that either parent raised the child.

key_assumptions.assumption: Spousal choice (marital assortment) is made independently of the status of the parents or siblings, i.e. matching is on the characteristics of the marital partners alone, so that the parent to child-in-law correlation equals θbr
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as 'entirely plausible' for modern Nordic countries (p. 4); no empirical test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The outcomes of the children of two siblings (cousins) are independent of each other given their own parents' status, so that the cousin correlation is θb²s and the aunt/uncle to niece/nephew correlation is θbs
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated when Fig. 1B is introduced; no separate test.

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: That 20-parameter model, in line with the results in Table 2, shows strong assortment in parenting, and strong persistence across generations.
Table 3 suggests that Denmark and Sweden have underlying social mobility rates that are similar, though not quite as high, as modern England, across all three dimensions of mobility.

claims.statement: Across OECD countries in PISA 2018 there is no association between a country's Gini coefficient for disposable income and the dispersion of its PISA scores: the Nordic countries, despite their low Gini and extensive public provision, have as high a dispersion of PISA scores as the average OECD country.

source_table.value: Figure 2, p. 11

mediators_claimed: Publicly subsidized pre-school for ages 1-5, where standards of care and education do not depend on parents' income
Compression of household income inequality, which should reduce variation in the material home environment of students

heterogeneity.finding: Nordic countries have as high a dispersion of PISA scores as the average OECD country, despite much lower income inequality.

ambiguities: The paper reports no coefficient, no fitted line and no statistical test for Figure 2, so point_estimate and statistically_significant are left null; the only printed value is the OECD average standard deviation of 94.7, recorded as the baseline mean.
The claim is a visual cross-country comparison offered as 'confirming evidence'; it is not identified by the paper's ratio method and bears on the mechanism rather than on the mobility parameters.

evidence.annotation: Notes: The dashed line shows the OECD average standard deviation of 94.7. The Gini coefficient is that for disposable income, averaged for 2012–2022

value.claimed_domain: Nordic countries' social provision and the within-cohort dispersion of scholastic performance
boundary_conditions: General performance-enhancing effects of more equal income distributions 'will have no effect on social mobility rates'

theory_referenced: The literature on the benefits of high-quality pre-school for children from the least advantaged families (Gormley et al. 2005; Heckman and Lochner 2000; Waldfogel 2006)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Earlier papers, which measured the amount of PISA score variation across students that can be predicted from such factors as the father's occupational class, confirm that societies with lower income inequality, such as the Nordics, are not associated with a decline in the gap in PISA scores

It has been claimed that more equal income distributions are associated with higher average achievement across countries (Condron 2011; Thorson and Gearhart 2018). But such general performance enhancing effects will have no effect on social mobility rates.
